books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, B. The Supreme Court Asserts Federal Power and the Power of the Judiciary

stimulus.source_note: Chief Justice John Marshall, Marbury v. Madison (1803), public domain. Abridged.
stimulus.text:
“It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is. Those who apply the rule to particular cases, must of necessity expound and interpret that rule. If two laws conflict with each other, the courts must decide on the operation of each.”
— Chief Justice John Marshall, Marbury v. Madison, 1803 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from Marbury v. Madison (1803)
stem: The case in the passage grew most directly out of which of the following?

options.text: Jefferson's purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France
options.misconception: The purchase raised questions about presidential power, but Marbury's suit was about a judgeship, not land.

options.text: Adams's last-minute judicial appointments, known as the midnight appointments
The Hartford Convention's call for constitutional amendments
options.misconception: The Hartford Convention met in 1814, eleven years after Marbury, and had nothing to do with it.

options.text: South Carolina's attempt to nullify the federal tariff
options.misconception: South Carolina nullified the tariff in 1832, decades after Marbury, in a different fight.

rationales.A: The purchase raised questions about presidential power, but Marbury's suit was about a judgeship, not land.
rationales.B: In his final weeks Adams filled new judgeships created by the Judiciary Act of 1801, and some commissions were never delivered. Jefferson ordered Madison not to deliver them, and Marbury, one of the appointees, sued for his. Background: Adams was packing the courts with Federalists before Jefferson took office, and Jefferson tried to undo it.
rationales.C: The Hartford Convention met in 1814, eleven years after Marbury, and had nothing to do with it.
rationales.D: South Carolina nullified the tariff in 1832, decades after Marbury, in a different fight.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who Marbury was. A man Adams appointed as a justice of the peace in the District of Columbia.
2. Ask why he sued. His commission was signed but never delivered.
3. Ask who stopped the delivery. Jefferson ordered Madison to hold the undelivered commissions.
4. Put it together. A last-minute appointment became the case that defined the Court.
Remember: a great court case usually starts as a small personal grievance, so find the person and the paper.
